question: Can a stabilized, GPU implementation of square independent component analysis provide a cheap first lens on language-model activations that is semantically inspectable and practically useful, and how much of the evidence establishes explanation plausibility, causal relevance, predictive validity, or adversarial faithfulness?

key_findings.claim: ICALens makes FastICA substantially more usable on residual streams, but its p95 acceptance rule deliberately retains a flagged non-converged tail and adaptive refitting gives different layers different representational resolutions.
key_findings.evidence: The pipeline row-normalizes each activation before centering and whitening, runs parallel GPU FastICA, accepts a strict fit when every component's LIM is below threshold, otherwise accepts when the 95th percentile is below threshold, and halves the component count until a fit is accepted. On GPT-2 Small with one million fitting rows, normalization plus the fallback accepts 10 of 12 residual layers versus 2 for raw strict fitting and uses 2,741 iterations; however, p95-accepted tail components remain in the artifact as unstable, and several Gemma/Qwen layers are reduced to one-quarter or one-half of hidden width.

key_findings.claim: The learned components are statistically exceptional relative to random and SAE directions, but excess kurtosis is evidence of non-Gaussian selectivity rather than semantic identity, independence, or causal use by the model.
key_findings.evidence: Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen3.5 2B Base, ICA score distributions have much larger excess kurtosis than 32,768 sampled random directions per layer and public SAE decoder directions; random projections cluster near zero while ICA commonly reaches tens to hundreds. Figure 3 reports signed excess kurtosis, not its absolute value. FastICA optimizes a log-cosh contrast after whitening, so this comparison establishes an unusual one-dimensional marginal. It does not test whether components are mutually independent in held-out activations, uniquely identifiable, semantically monosemantic, or used by downstream computation.

key_findings.claim: The effective receptive field diagnostic suggests a depth-dependent shift from token-local to contextual directions and a moderate inverse relation between kurtosis and required context, but both conclusions depend on several censoring and retrieval choices.
key_findings.evidence: For each top absolute activation, the analysis takes same-sign examples above half the maximum, tests suffixes of length 1 through 11, and calls a component recovered when it re-enters the top-15 absolute components with matching sign. Early layers have shorter ERFs and middle/deeper layers more values at the 11+ cap. ERF versus excess-kurtosis Spearman correlations are -0.50 for GPT-2 (n=7,981), -0.41 for Gemma (n=16,703), and -0.46 for Qwen (n=40,447). The top-15 rule, half-max sample filter, sign constraint, and right-censoring at 11 make ERF an operational probe, not an intrinsic context length or causal dependency.

anchors.section: 4.2 From Non-Gaussianity to Context Dependence / Figure 5

key_findings.claim: The human audit supports explanation plausibility for many randomly sampled components, but it is not a blinded semantic-validity or causal-faithfulness study.
key_findings.evidence: The authors randomly sample 50 components per model, inspect the dominant sign, top examples, contrastive prompts, and context ablations, and assign working labels. Of 150 components, 142 are labeled rather than unclear and 127 receive high confidence. A second expert reviews the high-confidence labels: 121 are supported, 6 partly supported, none rejected, and 112 receive at least 8/10 support. Both audits reuse the same component evidence and investigator-designed prompts, cover only the dominant side of a small random sample, and report no independent held-out annotator agreement or preregistered concept tests, so the results establish readable hypotheses rather than ground-truth semantics.

key_findings.claim: The polysemy, sentence-trace, and embedding-analogy figures demonstrate useful qualitative decompositions but also visibly show mixtures, associations, and analyst-selected cases rather than singular concepts.
key_findings.evidence: Across GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen, repeated financial-institution and river-edge uses of the token 'bank' decompose into different lexical, syntactic, semantic, positional, and discourse mixtures; selected GPT-2 traces also show components responding over spans. The fourth GPT-2 bank occurrence still carries finance-related components because only the contrastive prefix is available at that autoregressive position, illustrating that a component label is conditional on available context. The embedding examples include culturally loaded gender-associated analogy axes. These selected displays make behavior inspectable and falsifiable on nearby prompts, but provide neither population-level concept precision nor proof that a displayed label is a component's complete function.

key_findings.claim: On SAEBench sparse probing, ICA coordinates are competitive with the selected public SAEs and stronger than ITDA and PCA at the evaluated layers, but this is a supervised utility test rather than feature identifiability or native model faithfulness.
key_findings.evidence: Eight default SAEBench probing datasets are evaluated at two residual layers per model, splitting signed ICA scores into positive and negative coordinates. ICA generally beats ITDA and PCA and roughly matches public SAE curves; the Matryoshka SAE is included only for Gemma layer 12, and some SAE curves overtake ICA at larger feature budgets. Public dictionaries differ in width, training recipe, activation site, and capacity, while ICA itself has adaptively varying component counts, so the plots support usable labeled signal under a probe, not a matched claim that ICA recovers the model's true feature dictionary.

anchors.section: 6 Feature Utility under Sparse Probing and Intervention

key_findings.claim: Targeted Probe Perturbation is an intervention on reconstructed activations with a probe-defined outcome, not evidence that ICA components causally mediate native language-model behavior.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment zeroes the top-N feature coordinates selected by a concept probe, reconstructs through the ICA pseudoinverse, and measures the probe response. ICA produces stronger effects than public SAEs at small-to-medium N but degrades at larger N, where SAEs can be stronger. Because feature selection and evaluation share a supervised probe, the outcome is neither model loss nor generated behavior; the paper also cites concerns about the reliability of this benchmark. Thus the result tests coordinate-level control of a probe score, while native causal localization, semantic specificity, and off-target effects remain unmeasured.

key_findings.claim: Nearest-direction comparisons show partial ICA-SAE overlap and different token response profiles, not equivalence or superiority of one feature ontology.
key_findings.evidence: For each ICA write direction the paper reports maximum absolute cosine to a public SAE decoder; layer medians are broadly moderate, often around 0.4-0.5, with both closely aligned and weakly matched examples. Sampled tables compare selected low-, medium-, and high-overlap pairs. Token plots select highly active ICA and SAE features separately and row-normalize each response, with ICA often spanning related tokens and SAE features looking more localized. Cosine does not establish functional interchangeability, and the selection and independent normalization preclude comparing absolute sensitivity.

anchors.section: 7 How ICA Relates to SAEs / Figures 13-14

key_findings.claim: ICA's classical identifiability conditions and the paper's preprocessing choices leave the recovered axes contingent on the source model, sample distribution, normalization, component count, and optimization run.
key_findings.evidence: ICA identifies independent non-Gaussian sources only under a linear mixture model and up to sign/permutation; Gaussian or dependent sources and near-degenerate contrasts are not uniquely separated. Here the inputs are nonlinear residual representations, row normalization discards activation norm, whitening and fitting use one million Pile-10k positions, p95 acceptance tolerates unstable directions, and no multi-seed component matching or corpus-shift stability analysis is reported. Adaptive dimension reduction also makes the basis incomplete at difficult layers, with reconstruction through a pseudoinverse rather than an overcomplete sparse dictionary.

key_findings.claim: Across the evidence ladder, ICA Lens strongly supports a cheap, plausible exploratory lens, weakly-to-moderately supports supervised predictive utility, and does not establish adversarial faithfulness or native causal mediation.
key_findings.evidence: Human labels, contrastive prompts, ERF ablations, and qualitative traces test explanation plausibility. Sparse probing tests labeled predictive utility under an added classifier. TPP intervenes on reconstructed coordinates but reads out the same kind of probe rather than model behavior. There is no adversarial input search, explanation spoofing test, feature-edit effect on generation or loss, causal mediation comparison, held-out cross-corpus semantic validation, or demonstration that an ICA explanation predicts an unseen model failure. The paper appropriately concludes that ICA is a compact complement and first lens, not an SAE replacement.

method.core_idea: Fit a compact, square ICA basis independently to row-normalized activations from each embedding or residual-stream layer, then use signed component scores as read coordinates and a pseudoinverse as write directions for browsing, probing, and intervention-style tests.
method.mechanism: Row normalization limits norm outliers, whitening removes second-order correlations, and parallel FastICA rotates the whitened representation toward high log-cosh contrast/non-Gaussianity. A robust p95 convergence rule and component-count halving trade completeness for fit stability. ERF retrieval, human labeling, SAEBench probes, TPP, and SAE cosine comparisons then assess different notions of usefulness.
assumptions: Residual activations are adequately modeled as a linear mixture whose statistically independent or maximally non-Gaussian axes are meaningful features.
Row-normalized geometry is the relevant geometry even though token activation norms are discarded before fitting and writing.
One million uniformly sampled Pile-10k token positions adequately cover the sources of interest and do not privilege corpus-specific directions.
A p95-converged fit remains useful despite a known tail of components above the convergence threshold.
Adaptive reductions from d components down to d/2, d/4, or lower remain comparable across layers and models.
Signed scalar components are an appropriate ontology even for multidimensional, nonlinear, compositional, or distributed model features.
A pseudoinverse of the read map supplies valid write directions after normalization and dimensional reduction.
Probe utility and probe perturbation are informative proxies for interpretability despite not reading out native model behavior.
Public SAE checkpoints are sufficiently matched in activation site and model to be meaningful comparators despite different dictionary sizes and recipes.

techniques.role: Reduces activation-norm outliers and fits high-non-Gaussianity axes on GPU.
Accepts layers when most components converge while recording a difficult tail.
Halves target dimension until the layer passes the convergence rule.
Uses R=WK for component scores and D=R-pseudoinverse for reconstructed interventions.
Operationalizes how much suffix context is needed to reproduce a component ranking and sign.
Assigns and secondarily checks working semantic labels from retrieved examples and prompts.
Tests whether a small feature subset supports supervised concept prediction.
Zeroes probe-selected coordinates and reads the resulting change in probe score.
Measures directional overlap between ICA write axes and public SAE decoders.

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 Small residual layers with 1k to 1M fitting rows; raw versus row-normalized activations; strict max-LIM versus p95 fallback (pp. 8–10; pp. 34–35).
evaluations.metric: Accepted layers and total FastICA iterations, plus component-wise convergence traces.
evaluations.result: At 1M rows, normalized p95 fitting accepts 10/12 layers in 2,741 iterations versus raw strict fitting at 2/12 in 3,492; the fallback accepts a flagged unstable tail.
evaluations.baseline: Naive/raw parallel FastICA and strict all-component convergence.

evaluations.setting: Embedding and residual layers of GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen3.5 2B Base fitted from 1M Pile-10k token activations (pp. 10–13).
evaluations.metric: Excess kurtosis and operational ERF, compared with 32,768 random directions per layer and public SAE decoder directions.
evaluations.result: ICA directions are far more non-Gaussian than both comparison families; ERF generally grows with depth and correlates negatively with kurtosis at Spearman -0.41 to -0.50.
evaluations.baseline: Random directions and public SAE decoder directions.

evaluations.setting: Random audit of 50 components per model plus secondary review of high-confidence labels (pp. 15–18; pp. 39–44).
evaluations.metric: Labelability, confidence, prompt/ablation consistency, and expert support score.
evaluations.result: 142/150 receive a non-unclear label, 127 are high-confidence, and the second expert rates 121 supported and 6 partially supported; the evidence is shared rather than independently blinded.
evaluations.baseline: No formal random-direction, neuron, PCA, or blinded-annotator baseline in the human audit.

evaluations.setting: Eight SAEBench sparse-probing datasets at two layers for each of three models (pp. 23–24).
evaluations.metric: Probe performance versus number of selected coordinates.
evaluations.result: ICA is consistently stronger than PCA and ITDA and broadly competitive with the available public SAEs; some SAE curves become stronger at larger budgets.
evaluations.baseline: PCA, ITDA, public SAE, and one Matryoshka SAE setting.

evaluations.setting: SAEBench Targeted Probe Perturbation on GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen layers (pp. 24–25).
evaluations.metric: Change in a supervised probe score after ablating the top-N selected feature coordinates and reconstructing activations.
evaluations.result: ICA is relatively strongest at small-to-medium N and deteriorates at large N, where public SAEs can overtake it.
evaluations.baseline: Public SAEs under the same probe-defined perturbation metric.

evaluations.setting: All ICA components compared to public SAE decoder dictionaries, with sampled pair tables and selected token traces (pp. 26–28; p. 45).
evaluations.metric: Maximum absolute decoder cosine, layer median overlap, and normalized token activation profiles.
evaluations.result: Overlap is partial and broadly stable with depth; selected traces suggest ICA responses are often span-like while SAE responses are more token-local.
evaluations.baseline: Nearest feature in the model/layer's public SAE dictionary.

limitations: Author-stated: ICA is compact and at most hidden-width, so it cannot replace the resolution of a large overcomplete SAE dictionary.
Author-stated: not every layer converges at full width; adaptive refitting lowers dimensionality, and p95 acceptance leaves a difficult component tail.
Author-stated: TPP and sparse probing are imperfect proxies, and stronger native intervention evaluations are needed.
Reviewer-identified: the paper never verifies ICA's linear independent-source assumptions, mutual independence on held-out data, or component stability across seeds and corpora.
Reviewer-identified: row normalization improves optimization by deleting activation norm, which may itself carry causal or semantic signal and changes the space being explained.

Reviewer-identified: random human annotation covers only 150 components and generally the dominant sign; the second expert sees the same supporting evidence, so semantic validity is not independently established.
Reviewer-identified: public SAE comparisons are unmatched in capacity, training tokens, objective, width, and sometimes available layer coverage; adaptive ICA width further complicates comparisons.
Reviewer-identified: no reconstruction-fidelity curve, language-model loss, generation, task performance, or causal mediation test demonstrates that an ICA component is used by the native model.
Reviewer-identified: experiments stop at 2B-parameter models and one activation corpus, leaving scale, domain, architecture, and distribution transfer open.
Reviewer-identified: no adversarial or deception-aware test asks whether readable ICA axes stay faithful under optimized inputs, feature collisions, or explanation spoofing.
failure_modes: Dependent, Gaussian, multimodal, nonlinear, or multidimensional sources need not be separated into stable one-dimensional ICA components.
Nearly equal contrast optima can rotate across fitting seeds, making labels and write directions non-identifiable even when aggregate statistics reproduce.
Norm-coded information can disappear under row normalization, while pseudoinverse writes may move activations off the native residual distribution.
p95-accepted unstable components may generate spurious top examples or inconsistent interventions unless the tail flag is propagated to all analyses.
Adaptive component reduction can erase rare sources precisely in hard layers and produce misleading cross-layer trends in component counts or ERF.
A supervised probe can exploit incidental correlations in ICA scores; ablating its selected directions can change the probe without changing the model's own computation.
Human-readable top examples can arise from corpus co-occurrence, positional priors, or tokenization artifacts rather than a coherent causal concept.
Moderate SAE cosine overlap can hide sign, scaling, activation-threshold, and downstream-connectivity differences, so matched directions need not be functional substitutes.
Top-example retrieval and same-distribution prompt tests can miss rare polysemy and adversarial collisions that invalidate a concise component label.
reusable_insights: Treat ICA as a triage lens: use cheap non-Gaussian axes to choose layers and hypotheses before paying for an overcomplete dictionary.
Always keep convergence status at component granularity; never mix p95 tail components into semantic or intervention analyses without sensitivity checks.
Compare raw and row-normalized fits because optimization stability and explanatory target are different questions.
Separate statistical exceptionality, human labelability, supervised predictiveness, native causal effect, and adversarial faithfulness in any feature-evaluation dashboard.
Repeat component matching across seeds and corpora before treating an ICA axis as identifiable; report subspace stability when individual axes rotate.
Evaluate write directions with native loss/behavior and off-target metrics, not only a probe that selected the direction.
When comparing square ICA with overcomplete SAEs, match coordinate budgets and reconstruction distortion or state explicitly that the methods target different resolutions.
Use the ERF idea as an operational context diagnostic, but publish threshold, rank, sign, and censoring sensitivity rather than one scalar as an intrinsic property.
open_questions: Are ICA axes stable under fitting seed, corpus, token-frequency reweighting, row-normalization choice, and model checkpoint, or only their spanned subspaces?
Does an ICA component intervention cause selective changes in native next-token probabilities or generated behavior after matching activation distortion to an SAE intervention?
Can overcomplete or nonlinear ICA retain the training-light advantage while resolving more than d sources and multidimensional features?
Does ERF predict which components support cross-domain behavioral generalization, or merely which top examples are lexically recoverable?
Can held-out human concept datasets and adversarially generated counterexamples quantify label completeness, collision rates, and negative-side semantics?
How much of ICA's apparent advantage over public SAEs remains after matching feature budget, reconstruction error, activation site, training corpus, and probe selection procedure?
Do high-kurtosis directions predict causal model mechanisms, or can equivalent model behavior be supported by low-kurtosis distributed subspaces?
Can convergence uncertainty be incorporated into downstream probes and interventions rather than treated as a binary layer-level accept/reject decision?

competitive_landscape.title: Concept Component Analysis: A Principled Approach for Concept Extraction in LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest prior unsupervised linear-unmixing method for LLM activations
competitive_landscape.difference: Sparse ConCA derives a linear-mixture view of LLM representations from a latent-variable model of concept log-posteriors and evaluates twelve sparse unmixing variants. ICA Lens instead applies classical non-Gaussian FastICA without ConCA's concept-posterior derivation, but contributes a more complete layer-wise fitting, browsing, human-audit, probing, and intervention workflow.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering Universal Geometry in Embeddings with ICA
competitive_landscape.difference: Yamagiwa et al. already use ICA to expose interpretable semantic axes in pretrained word and image embeddings and compare their alignment across languages, algorithms, and modalities. ICA Lens extends ICA from static embeddings to contextual residual streams, adds LLM-specific convergence engineering, and evaluates supervised feature utility, so its novelty is the practical LLM-activation workflow rather than interpretable ICA axes per se.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring Interpretability of Independent Components of Word Embeddings with Automated Word Intruder Test
competitive_landscape.relationship: prior human and automated audit of ICA components
competitive_landscape.difference: Musil and Marecek quantify ICA word-embedding interpretability with both human and LLM word-intruder tests and show component combinations support lexical retrieval. ICA Lens evaluates contextual LLM states and richer prompt/ERF/SAEBench evidence, but is not the first systematic human-facing evaluation of ICA-derived language representations.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Higher-Order Correlations Among Semantic Components in Embeddings
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct negative evidence on the independence interpretation
competitive_landscape.difference: Oyama et al. explicitly show that semantically meaningful higher-order dependencies remain among ICA embedding components and visualize their dependency structure. ICA Lens measures one-dimensional kurtosis and semantic usefulness but never tests residual mutual or higher-order dependence, so 'independent components' should not be read as empirically verified independent sources.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Cunningham et al. train an overcomplete sparse reconstruction dictionary and test causal responsibility on IOI; ICA Lens avoids dictionary training and returns at most hidden-width signed axes, but does not reproduce the native behavioral causal test.

competitive_landscape.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
competitive_landscape.relationship: evaluation framework and partial benchmark source
competitive_landscape.difference: SAEBench evaluates more than 200 SAEs across eight metrics and finds proxy gains do not reliably transfer to practical tasks; ICA Lens imports sparse probing and TPP subsets but does not run the suite's full disentanglement, unlearning, or application battery.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
competitive_landscape.difference: Kantamneni et al. stress-test sparse probing under scarcity, imbalance, noise, and shift and find strong non-SAE ensembles usually match SAEs; ICA Lens reports standard probing curves but does not test those harder regimes or whether ICA adds value beyond an ensemble of raw-activation baselines.

competitive_landscape.title: Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA): A Scalable Approach to Interpreting Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ITDA greedily builds activation dictionaries with matching pursuit using about 1% of SAE time/data and demonstrates 70B/405B and cross-model comparisons; ICA Lens is simpler and stronger on its selected probes but is fit independently per model and evaluated only through 2B scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Qwen-Scope: Turning Sparse Features into Development Tools for Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Qwen-Scope releases SAEs for seven dense and MoE Qwen variants and evaluates steering, evaluation analysis, data workflows, SFT, and RL uses; ICA Lens analyzes one 2B Qwen model and stops at probe-defined intervention rather than native development workflows.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Matryoshka SAEs jointly preserve general features in small nested dictionaries and specific features at larger widths, with probing and targeted erasure evidence; ICA Lens has one square-or-reduced resolution per layer and cannot represent a comparable hierarchy.

competitive_landscape.title: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: BatchTopK allocates a variable number of active latents per example while directly controlling average sparsity and improves reconstruction over TopK; ICA Lens uses dense signed square coordinates and maximizes non-Gaussianity rather than reconstruction or adaptive per-example sparsity.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Gated SAEs separate feature selection from magnitude estimation to reduce L1 shrinkage and report reconstruction/interpretability tradeoffs through 7B models; ICA Lens has no learned gate, explicit sparse code, or matched reconstruction-fidelity evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: JumpReLU directly optimizes L0 sparsity with a discontinuous activation and achieves high reconstruction fidelity at fixed sparsity; ICA Lens trades overcomplete reconstruction for a cheap non-Gaussian basis and therefore needs a distortion-matched native-behavior comparison before superiority claims.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
competitive_landscape.difference: Arora et al. show that pre-down-projection MLP neurons can be as sparse as SAE features for circuit tracing and give native causal and steering evidence on subject-verb agreement and city-state-capital relations without additional feature training. ICA Lens instead rotates residual streams for layer-wide semantic browsing and probe utility, but does not supply comparable native-behaviour circuit evidence; the current neuron-basis result further narrows any implication that a learned or fitted rotation is required for training-free interpretability.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A practical, stable, auditable ICA workflow reveals interpretable LLM activation structure without training another dictionary and is competitive with public SAEs on selected feature-utility benchmarks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The main novelty is the integration of row normalization, component-wise p95 convergence, adaptive refitting, an explorer, ERF, human audits, and selected SAEBench evaluations across three small model families. ICA and FastICA are classical; prior work already demonstrated interpretable ICA axes and human/automated ICA audits for language embeddings, sparse ConCA already applied theory-motivated unsupervised linear unmixing to LLM representations, and current neuron-basis work supplies a different training-free route with native causal circuit evidence. Several comparison metrics and public dictionaries are also inherited.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The workflow contribution is credible and useful as low-cost triage, particularly its LLM-specific convergence diagnostics and integration of contextual inspection with selected benchmarks. The strongest defensible novelty is a practical, auditable FastICA workflow for contextual LLM residual-stream activations, not the discovery that ICA yields interpretable language directions, the first unsupervised linear unmixing of LLM states, or the only training-free alternative to learned dictionaries. Evidence supports explanation plausibility and supervised coordinate utility, but not source identifiability, native causal mediation, adversarial faithfulness, or a matched replacement for SAEs or native-neuron circuit analyses. Claims should remain 'first lens' rather than 'feature recovery.'

reviewer_notes: Independent secondary verification read all 47 pages of the exact indexed arXiv v1 paper, including references, Appendices A-F, complete random-label and secondary-audit tables, fitting diagnostics, token plots, and screenshots; central figures, equations, and tables were also inspected in the rendered PDF. Every finding, anchor, evaluation, novelty boundary, limitation, negative result, and contradiction claim was rechecked. The pass corrected the metric description from absolute to signed excess kurtosis and retained the earlier correction from four bank senses to the paper's financial-versus-river experiment. Evidence categories remain distinct: plausibility is strong, predictive validity is limited to supervised probes, native-behaviour causal localisation is absent, and adversarial faithfulness is untested. Fourteen version-pinned primary competitors are recorded, including prior ICA and linear-unmixing work, higher-order-dependence counterevidence, and a current training-free neuron-basis alternative.
